I have an uncle with down syndrome. He's in his 60's with the mind of a child. I don't know what I would do in the situation, so I can't really answer the question, but I do want to share a bit about my families experience.

Sometimes I feel sad for my grandmother. She's had to take care of a child for her entire adult life. There was no looking forward to a day when he would move out and my grand parents would be able to enjoy their old age with no distractions. I'm sure there are struggles as the years go by, where you think about how much longer your child will live, and maybe hope for everyone sake it isn't much longer. I mentioned that my uncle is 60, so his younger age was before there were programs in every city for those with mental disabilities.

He's had a job, and used to go to school where he could create relationships with people with similar conditions. He shaves and knows how to do his daily duties. It's mostly routine for him now. He is greatly influenced by television, so whereas the rest of us struggle to change our eating habits, we have to pretend like all food is good for you or he will just stop eating due to the amount of television that reminds us that dieting is very important. We thought he was going to starve himself at one point, because he wouldn't eat. He would always say he was on a diet. My mom came up with the idea that we should take him to a restaurant, and the whole family would talk about how delicious the food is. This is how we got him to eat french fries, and then eventually more food. It's one of those struggles you wouldn't foresee. He's gained his weight back, and is a lot healthier.

Simultaneously, he also brings so much joy into our lives. Since his mind state is so young, he looks at the world with eyes of wonder. Whenever we visit, he comes out of his room and gives the biggest smile as he hugs everyone. He's genuinely happy to see us. Just having a conversation with him about Batman makes his day. He'll update you on the latest things to happen on Star Trek or the Brady Bunch, and just laugh as if he was watching it for the first time.

A major benefit to having him in our life is we never get the opportunity to lose the Christmas spirit. If you open gifts with your family, you know what it'slike to have a bunch of adults sitting around opening presents from each other. Those moments before opening a gift where you prepare yourself to appreciate whatever is inside. The thing is, with my uncle, there is none of that. He opens the gift, and loves whatever is inside. It doesn't matter what it is at all. It's just that you got him a present. He loves you for it, he loves whatever the gift was. Each present, his eyes get big, he gasps and smiles the largest smile you have ever seen. It's those moments that you realize the things you have outgrown are still present in a man that has gone through it many times before. That wide-eyed wonder of the world.

My views are going to be controversial, but that is expected with a question such as this.

Mental disability has come to be seen as an undesirable trait that should be culled from humanity. It is understandable that this kind of position has emerged, because at a deep evolutionary level we are wired to fear diseases and to be much more accepting of traits that are perceived as providing value to the survival of the species and a conservation of resources.

However, our instinctual dislike of genetic differences are not always logical, and with technology increasing at exponential rates we are fast approaching a post-scarcity society where people who would classically not have survived or had a high quality of life can and often do go on to live happy fulfilling lives. Not to mention all of the assistive technologies coming out with the potential to cure debilitating brain defects.

I am of the opinion that very soon, in the next couple decades, it will be just as easy to provide technology to people born with debilitating mental states to enable them to be just as capable as the person born with a perfectly healthy brain as it is for us to provide technology to people missing a limb enabling them to be as capable as someone with a perfectly healthy body. However, even if we never are able to invent assistive technologies, imagining that we are smart enough right now to demand the right to decide someone else's life is meaningless has the potential to turn more of us into cold, instinctual, impulsive sociopaths.

If you are seriously thinking that aborting your child because of an early-detected birth defect is perfectly fine regardless of our ability to cure him or her or provide them with a higher quality of life, you probably should not be actively trying to bring a child into our quickly changing world. Also, it probably wouldn't hurt you to watch the movie "Gattaca" and give real thought into what your current mindset means and how far you are willing to carry out your eugenics.
